questions.stem: You can see a wooden chair in a lit room. Which statement describes how you see it?

options.text: Light from the lamp reflects off the chair and enters your eye
Your eye sends out rays that strike the chair
The chair produces its own light which reaches your eye
The chair must be hot for you to see it

questions.explanation: Non-luminous objects are seen by diffusely reflecting light from a source into the eye.

questions.stem: Why can you not see around a corner, even in a brightly lit corridor?

options.text: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium
Rays from the eye cannot turn corners
Light is absorbed completely by the wall
Light slows down near solid objects

questions.explanation: Rectilinear propagation means light does not bend round an obstacle at everyday scales.

questions.stem: A ray strikes a plane mirror at 30 degrees to the mirror surface. What is the angle of reflection?

options.text: 60 degrees
30 degrees
120 degrees
The ray passes into the mirror and bends

questions.explanation: Angles are measured from the normal, so the angle of incidence is 90 - 30 = 60 degrees, and reflection equals it.

questions.stem: Which quantities always lie in one plane for a reflected ray?

options.text: Incident ray, reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence
Incident ray, refracted ray and the mirror surface
Only the incident and reflected rays
The normal and the mirror surface only

questions.explanation: The second law of reflection states all three lie in the same plane.

questions.stem: You stand 2 m from a plane mirror. How far is your image from you?

options.text: 4 m
2 m
1 m
It depends on the size of the mirror

questions.explanation: The image is 2 m behind the mirror, so it is 4 m from you.

questions.stem: Which set correctly describes the image in a plane mirror?

options.text: Virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
Real, erect, same size, formed on the mirror surface
Virtual, inverted, magnified
Real, inverted, diminished

questions.explanation: A plane mirror always gives a virtual, erect, same-sized, laterally inverted image as far behind as the object is in front.

questions.stem: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 24 cm. What is its focal length?

options.text: 12 cm
24 cm
48 cm
6 cm

questions.explanation: For a spherical mirror f = R/2 = 12 cm.

questions.stem: The centre of curvature of a concave mirror lies 30 cm from the pole. Where is the principal focus?

options.text: 15 cm from the pole, in front of the mirror
30 cm from the pole, coinciding with the centre of curvature
15 cm behind the mirror
At the pole itself

questions.explanation: F is the midpoint of P and C, so 15 cm in front for a concave mirror.

questions.stem: An object is placed between the pole and the focus of a concave mirror. The image is:

options.text: Virtual, erect and enlarged
Real, inverted and enlarged
Real, inverted and diminished
Formed exactly on the mirror surface

questions.explanation: Inside the focus the reflected rays diverge, so only their extensions meet: a virtual, erect, magnified image. This is the shaving-mirror case.

questions.stem: An object sits at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. The image is:

options.text: At C, real, inverted and the same size
At F, real, inverted and diminished
Behind the mirror, virtual and erect
On the mirror surface, same size

questions.explanation: At C the image returns to C, real, inverted, equal in size.

questions.stem: A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object placed 20 cm in front. Using the sign convention, the image distance v is:

options.text: -60 cm, so the image is 60 cm in front of the mirror
+60 cm, so the image is 60 cm behind the mirror
+30 cm, since f equals R

questions.explanation: With u = -20 and f = -15, 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/15 + 1/20 = -1/60, giving v = -60 cm: real, in front.

questions.stem: For a convex mirror, which statement about the signs is correct for a real object?

options.text: u is negative while f and v are positive
All of u, v and f are positive
All of u, v and f are negative
f is negative because the mirror curves outward

questions.explanation: Distances measured against the incident light are negative; a convex mirror's focus and virtual image lie behind it, so f and v are positive.

questions.stem: A mirror produces a magnification of -3 for a 2 cm object. The image is:

options.text: 6 cm tall and inverted
About 0.67 cm tall and inverted
6 cm tall and erect
2 cm tall and inverted

questions.explanation: The modulus of m gives the size ratio (3x, so 6 cm); the minus sign means inverted.

questions.stem: A convex mirror used as a vehicle rear-view mirror gives a magnification of +0.5. The image is:

options.text: Erect and half the size of the object
Inverted and half the size
Erect and twice the size
The same size but reversed

questions.explanation: Positive m means erect; 0.5 means half the size, which is why convex mirrors give a wide field of view.

questions.stem: Light passes from air into water. What actually causes it to change direction?

options.text: Its speed changes at the boundary between the media
It bounces off the water surface
Its speed is the same but the water pushes it sideways
Water particles absorb and re-emit it randomly

questions.explanation: Refraction arises because light travels at different speeds in different media.

questions.stem: A ray travels from air into a glass block, striking the surface obliquely. It bends:

options.text: Toward the normal, because glass is optically denser
Away from the normal, because glass is optically denser
Not at all, since its speed is unchanged
Back into the air along the same path

questions.explanation: Entering a denser medium light slows and bends toward the normal.

questions.stem: The refractive index of water is 1.33. The speed of light in water is about:

options.text: 3 x 10^8 m/s, the same as in air

questions.explanation: v = c/n = 3 x 10^8 / 1.33, which is about 2.26 x 10^8 m/s.

questions.stem: What is the unit of refractive index?

options.text: It has no unit
m/s
dioptre
metre

questions.explanation: It is the ratio of two speeds, so the units cancel.

questions.stem: Light goes from glass (n = 1.5) into air. Compared with the incident ray, the refracted ray:

options.text: Bends away from the normal
Bends toward the normal
Continues undeviated regardless of the angle
Is reflected back into the glass at every angle

questions.explanation: Going into a rarer medium light speeds up and bends away from the normal.

questions.stem: A ray enters a medium at 45 degrees to the normal and refracts at 30 degrees. The refractive index is about:
questions.explanation: n = sin 45 / sin 30 = 0.707 / 0.5, which is about 1.41.

questions.stem: A ray passes obliquely through a rectangular glass slab. The emergent ray is:

options.text: Parallel to the incident ray but laterally displaced
Bent further away from the original direction
Reflected back along the incident path
Perpendicular to the incident ray

questions.explanation: The two parallel surfaces produce equal and opposite bends, so direction is restored with a sideways shift.

questions.stem: Lateral displacement through a glass slab increases when:

options.text: The slab is made thicker
The ray strikes exactly along the normal
The refractive index is reduced toward 1
The slab is cooled so light speeds up inside

questions.explanation: Displacement grows with thickness, angle of incidence and refractive index; at normal incidence it is zero.

questions.stem: Which lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges and converges a parallel beam?

options.text: Convex lens
Concave lens
Both converge a parallel beam
Neither, lenses only reflect light

questions.explanation: A convex lens is thicker centrally and brings parallel rays to a real focus.

questions.stem: Which statement about a convex lens is true?

options.text: It can form a diminished image when the object is beyond 2F
It always forms an enlarged image
It always forms a virtual image
It diverges every incident beam

questions.explanation: Beyond 2F the image is real, inverted and diminished; magnification depends on object position.

questions.stem: An object is at 2F of a convex lens. The image is:

options.text: At 2F on the other side, real, inverted and the same size
At F, real, inverted and enlarged
At infinity
Virtual and erect on the same side

questions.explanation: Object at 2F gives an image at 2F, equal in size and inverted.

questions.stem: An object is placed between F and the optical centre of a convex lens. The image is:

options.text: Virtual, erect and enlarged, on the same side as the object
Real, inverted and enlarged on the far side
Real and diminished at F
Always the same size as the object

questions.explanation: This is the magnifying glass case: rays diverge after the lens, so the image is virtual, erect and magnified.

questions.stem: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm has an object 15 cm away. The image distance v is:

options.text: +30 cm, real and on the opposite side
-30 cm, virtual and on the same side
+6 cm
+25 cm

questions.stem: For the lens above, the magnification is -2. This means the image is:

options.text: Twice as tall as the object and inverted
Half as tall and inverted
Twice as tall and erect
The same height but reversed left to right

questions.explanation: m = v/u = 30/(-15) = -2, so twice the size and inverted.

questions.stem: A convex lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Its power is:
questions.explanation: P = 1/f with f in metres: 1/0.20 = +5 D.

questions.stem: Two thin lenses of powers +4 D and -6 D are placed in contact. The combination is:

options.text: A diverging lens of focal length about 50 cm
A converging lens of focal length about 10 cm
A diverging lens of power -24 D
A converging lens of power +0.02 D

questions.explanation: Powers add: P = 4 - 6 = -2 D, so f = -0.5 m, a diverging combination of focal length 50 cm.

questions.stem: Which part of the eye controls the amount of light entering it?

options.text: The iris, by changing the size of the pupil
The cornea
The retina
The optic nerve

questions.explanation: The iris is the coloured muscular diaphragm that adjusts the pupil aperture.

questions.stem: Where is a real, inverted image formed inside the human eye?

options.text: On the retina
On the cornea
At the pupil
On the eye lens surface itself

questions.explanation: The cornea and lens together focus light onto the light-sensitive retina.

questions.stem: How does the eye focus on a nearby object after looking at a distant one?

options.text: Ciliary muscles contract, thickening the lens and shortening its focal length
The lens moves forward toward the cornea
The retina moves backward
The pupil closes completely

questions.explanation: Accommodation changes lens curvature, not lens position.

questions.stem: The least distance of distinct vision for a normal adult eye is about:

options.text: 25 cm
2.5 cm
Infinity

questions.explanation: The near point of a normal eye is roughly 25 cm; the far point is at infinity.

questions.stem: A student cannot see the blackboard clearly but reads a book easily. The defect and its correction are:

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a concave lens
Myopia, corrected with a convex lens
Hypermetropia, corrected with a concave lens
Presbyopia, corrected with a bifocal lens

questions.explanation: In myopia the image falls in front of the retina, so a diverging (concave) lens is needed.

questions.stem: A hypermetropic eye has a near point of 50 cm. The power of the correcting lens for a 25 cm near point is:
questions.explanation: With u = -25 cm and v = -50 cm, 1/f = 1/v - 1/u gives f = +50 cm, so P = +2 D.

questions.stem: White light passed through a prism splits into colours because:

options.text: Different wavelengths are refracted through different angles
The prism adds colour to the white light
The glass reflects each colour separately
White light has no colour until it meets glass

questions.explanation: White light is already composite; the prism separates components because refractive index varies with wavelength.

questions.stem: In the visible spectrum produced by a prism, which colour deviates most?

options.text: Violet
Red
Green
All deviate equally

questions.explanation: Violet has the shortest wavelength and the largest refractive index, so it bends most.

questions.stem: Stars appear to twinkle but planets generally do not. Why?

options.text: Stars are point sources, so varying atmospheric refraction changes their apparent brightness
Stars physically pulse in brightness
Planets are much hotter than stars
Planets emit a steadier kind of light

questions.explanation: Planets are extended sources whose many points average out the fluctuations.

questions.stem: The sun is visible about two minutes before actual sunrise because:

options.text: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight, raising the sun's apparent position
The sun physically rises earlier than calculated
Sunlight is reflected off high clouds
Light travels faster through the upper atmosphere

questions.explanation: Increasing air density toward the ground bends rays, so the sun appears higher than it is.

questions.stem: The sky appears blue mainly because:

options.text: Shorter wavelengths are scattered more strongly by air molecules
The sky reflects the colour of the oceans
Air molecules emit blue light
Blue light travels fastest through air

questions.explanation: Scattering grows sharply as wavelength falls, so blue dominates the scattered sky light.

questions.stem: The sun looks reddish at sunrise and sunset because:

options.text: Light travels a longer path, so most blue is scattered away
The sun is cooler at those times
The atmosphere reflects red light back
Red light is scattered most near the horizon

questions.explanation: The long slant path removes short wavelengths, leaving the transmitted light red.

questions.stem: A charge of 6 C flows past a point in 2 s. The current is:

options.text: 3 A
3 A entering and 1.5 A leaving the bulb

questions.stem: In a simple series circuit with one bulb, how does the current just before the bulb compare with the current just after it?

options.text: They are equal, because charge is conserved
It is smaller after, because the bulb uses up current
It is larger after, because the bulb heats the charges
There is no current after the bulb

questions.explanation: The bulb transfers energy, not charge; current is the same throughout a series loop.

questions.stem: The potential difference across a component is defined as:

options.text: Work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points
The amount of current used up in the component
The total charge stored in the component
The resistance divided by the current

questions.explanation: V = W/Q, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).

questions.stem: Moving 10 C between two points takes 60 J of work. The potential difference is:

options.text: 6 V

questions.stem: A 12 V supply drives 3 A through a resistor. Its resistance is:

options.text: 4 ohm
36 ohm
0.25 ohm
15 ohm

questions.stem: A graph of V against I for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature is:

options.text: A straight line through the origin whose slope is the resistance
A curve bending toward the I axis
A horizontal straight line
A straight line whose slope is the current

questions.explanation: Ohm's law gives V proportional to I, so the slope V/I is the resistance.

questions.stem: A uniform wire is replaced by one of the same material and length but twice the cross-sectional area. Its resistance:

options.text: Halves
Doubles
Stays the same
Quadruples

questions.explanation: R = rho L / A, so resistance is inversely proportional to area.

questions.stem: A wire is stretched so its length doubles while its volume stays constant. Its new resistance is:

options.text: Four times the original
Twice the original
Half the original
Unchanged, since resistivity is unchanged

questions.explanation: Doubling L halves A at constant volume, and R = rho L/A, so R rises by a factor of 4.

questions.stem: Resistors of 2 ohm, 3 ohm and 5 ohm are joined in series. The equivalent resistance is:

options.text: 10 ohm
0.97 ohm
1.03 ohm
3.33 ohm

questions.explanation: In series resistances add directly.

questions.stem: Three unequal resistors are in series across a battery. Which quantity is the same for all three?

options.text: The current
The potential difference
The power dissipated
Both current and potential difference

questions.explanation: Series means one path, so current is common and the supply voltage divides in proportion to resistance.

questions.stem: A 6 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor are connected in parallel. The equivalent resistance is:

options.text: 2 ohm
9 ohm
4.5 ohm
18 ohm

questions.explanation: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohm, less than the smaller resistor.

questions.stem: Two unequal resistors are in parallel across a 12 V battery. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Each has 12 V across it, and the smaller resistor carries the larger current
Each carries the same current, and the voltage divides between them
The voltage divides in proportion to resistance
The total resistance is the sum of the two

questions.explanation: Parallel branches share the same potential difference; current divides inversely with resistance.

questions.stem: The current through a fixed resistor is doubled. The heat produced in the same time becomes:

options.text: Four times as much
Twice as much
Half as much
Unchanged

questions.explanation: H = I squared R t, so heat scales with the square of the current.

questions.stem: Why is tungsten used for the filament of an incandescent lamp?

options.text: High resistivity and a very high melting point
Low resistivity so it heats quickly
It conducts heat away rapidly
Its resistivity falls as it is drawn thinner

questions.explanation: The filament must glow without melting, so high resistivity and a melting point above 3000 C are needed.

questions.stem: A bulb is marked 100 W, 220 V. The current it draws at rated voltage is about:
questions.explanation: P = VI, so I = 100/220, which is about 0.45 A.

questions.stem: A 1000 W heater runs for 2 hours daily. The energy used in 30 days is:

options.text: 60 kWh
2 kWh
0.06 kWh

questions.explanation: 1 kW x 2 h x 30 = 60 kWh, the commercial unit of electrical energy.

questions.stem: Why can two magnetic field lines never intersect?

options.text: The field would then have two directions at one point, which is impossible
They repel because both carry north poles
They can intersect at the poles
Intersections only occur inside the magnet

questions.explanation: The tangent gives the unique field direction, so crossing lines are impossible.

questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from north to south. Inside the magnet they:

options.text: Run from south to north, completing closed loops
Stop at the poles and do not continue
Also run from north to south
Are absent, since the field exists only outside

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed curves.

questions.stem: A straight wire carries current vertically upward. The magnetic field around it is:

options.text: Concentric circles in a horizontal plane, given by the right-hand thumb rule
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Circles that cross one another near the wire
Radial lines pointing away from the wire

questions.explanation: Point the right thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the circular field direction.

questions.stem: The current in a straight conductor is doubled and the distance from it is also doubled. The magnetic field strength at that point:

options.text: Stays the same
Doubles
Quadruples
Becomes one quarter

questions.explanation: B is proportional to I and inversely proportional to r, so the two changes cancel.

questions.stem: The field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is:

options.text: Uniform and parallel to the axis, like that of a bar magnet
Zero everywhere inside
Circular around the axis
Strongest at the exact centre and zero at the ends

questions.explanation: A solenoid produces a nearly uniform axial interior field and behaves externally like a bar magnet.

questions.stem: Placing a soft iron core inside a solenoid produces an electromagnet because the core:

options.text: Becomes strongly magnetised and intensifies the field
Increases the current in the coil
Prevents the field lines from closing
Stores charge for later release

questions.explanation: Soft iron magnetises readily and loses magnetism when current stops, which is what an electromagnet needs.

questions.stem: Which rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?

options.text: Fleming's left-hand rule
Fleming's right-hand rule
The right-hand thumb rule
Lenz's law

questions.explanation: Left hand for the motor effect; right hand is for induced current in a generator.

questions.stem: A conductor carries current parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The force on it is:

options.text: Zero
Maximum, given by the left-hand rule
Maximum, given by the right-hand rule
Directed along the current

questions.explanation: Force is greatest when current is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel to it.

questions.stem: A bar magnet is pushed into a closed coil that contains no battery. What happens?

options.text: A current is induced while the magnet is moving
Nothing, because the coil has no source of emf
A steady current flows even after the magnet stops
The coil becomes permanently magnetised

questions.explanation: A changing magnetic flux induces a current; relative motion, not a battery, is what is required.

questions.stem: In an AC generator, the direction of the induced current is found using:

options.text: Fleming's right-hand rule
Fleming's left-hand rule
The right-hand thumb rule for a straight conductor
The sign convention for mirrors

questions.explanation: Generators use the right-hand rule; motors use the left.

questions.stem: In a domestic circuit, the earth wire:

options.text: Provides a low-resistance path to the ground if a fault makes the appliance casing live
Carries the return current during normal operation
Supplies the appliance with current
Replaces the need for a fuse

questions.explanation: The neutral wire carries the return current; the earth wire is a safety path used only on a fault.

questions.stem: A fuse is connected in the live wire because:

options.text: It must break the live connection to isolate the appliance on overload
The live wire carries less current than the neutral
Fuses only work at earth potential
It increases the current to blow faster

questions.explanation: A fuse in the neutral would cut the return path but leave the appliance live, which is dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of these is a conventional source of energy?

options.text: Coal
Solar cell
Wind turbine
Biogas plant

questions.explanation: Fossil fuels and large hydro are the conventional sources; the rest are non-conventional.

questions.stem: A thermal power plant is usually sited near a coalfield rather than near the consumer because:

options.text: Transmitting electricity is more efficient than transporting bulk coal
Coal burns better at the mine
Electricity cannot be transmitted over long distances
It avoids all environmental impact

questions.explanation: Moving energy as electricity costs less than hauling large masses of fuel.

questions.stem: Which statement about nuclear energy is correct?

options.text: It is non-renewable, since uranium reserves are finite
It is renewable, because the reaction sustains itself
It produces no waste requiring long-term storage
It is a conventional source with zero environmental cost

questions.explanation: Nuclear fuel is exhaustible and the waste stays hazardous for a very long time.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about solar cells?

options.text: Generation is clean, but manufacture uses energy and special materials
They have no environmental cost at any stage
They work equally well at night
They are classed as a conventional source

questions.explanation: Solar is renewable with clean operation, but silicon processing and silver contacts carry real costs.
